facts.claim: Pro Git: at its core Git is a simple store of content by key: put in any content and Git hands back a unique key to get it out again later.
Pro Git: Git names an object by the SHA-1 checksum of a header (its type, a space, its size in bytes and a null byte) followed by its content.
Git’s config docs: by default Git shortens a name to a length it picks from the repository’s size, long enough to stay unique for some time; the shortest is 4 characters.
Pro Git: a tree stores file names and groups files together; each entry is the hash of a blob or subtree with its mode, type and file name.
Pro Git: a commit names the top-level tree of its snapshot, its parent commits if any, the author and committer with a timestamp, then a blank line and the message.
Pro Git: a branch in Git is simply a lightweight movable pointer to one of the commits.
Pro Git: creating a new branch is as quick as writing 41 bytes to a file (40 characters and a newline).
Pro Git: HEAD is a pointer to the local branch you are currently on.
Pro Git: Git does a simple three-way merge, using the two snapshots at the branch tips and their common ancestor.
Pro Git: the result is a merge commit, special in that it has more than one parent.
Pro Git: if you changed the same part of the same file differently in the two branches, Git can’t merge them cleanly.
Pro Git: a rebase takes the changes committed on one branch and replays them on another, abandoning the old commits for new ones that are similar but different.
Pro Git’s rule: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.
Pro Git: a rebase replays the changes of one line of work in the order they were made, whereas a merge takes the two ends and merges them together.
Stevens, Bursztein, Karpman, Albertini and Markov (2017) made the first known SHA-1 collision: two different PDF files with the same hash.
Git’s hash-function transition plan: after the 23 February 2017 SHA-1 collision, Git moved to a hardened SHA-1 by default (v2.13.0), and in late 2018 picked SHA-256 as its successor.
Git’s init docs, as checked in October 2026: a new repository can use sha1 or sha256, and sha1 is still the default.
